title: Fournier’s Gangrene Surgical Reconstruction: A Systematic Review
clinical_background: FG is an uncommon, rapidly progressive necrotizing infection of the perineal, genital or perianal region, with reported mortality exceeding 20%. It usually affects men older than 50 years. Immediate resuscitation, intravenous antibiotics and early surgical debridement are required. Reconstruction may be needed to cover exposed testicles, preserve their function and restore appearance while limiting morbidity and mortality. The optimal timing and choice of reconstructive procedure remain debated, and precise guidelines are unavailable.
objectives: Systematically examine contemporary surgical reconstruction approaches for FG and assess the available strategies and their specific indications.
clinical_question: In patients with FG (P), what reconstructive outcomes and complications (O) are associated with surgery and surgical reconstruction (I), compared with a control group, a nonsurgical strategy or medical treatment (C)?
study_design: Systematic review conducted according to PRISMA. PubMed (MEDLINE), EMBASE, Cochrane, Web of Science, and Scopus were searched for studies published from April 2014 to April 2024. Titles, abstracts, and potentially eligible full texts were screened against the selection criteria; bibliographic references were also checked. The review was registered in PROSPERO as CRD42024555882.

population.description: Patients with Fournier’s gangrene who underwent surgical treatment in the included studies.
inclusion_criteria: Original observational studies or randomized controlled trials addressing surgical treatment of Fournier’s gangrene.
Case series reporting at least three Fournier’s gangrene cases.

interventions: Surgery and surgical reconstruction for Fournier’s gangrene.
comparators: Control group, as specified in the review’s PICO framework.
Non-surgical strategies, as specified in the review’s PICO framework.
Medical treatment, as specified in the review’s PICO framework.
interpretation: The authors conclude that most reconstructive defects caused by Fournier’s gangrene can be managed with less invasive approaches, particularly skin grafts and local random flaps, despite the potentially extensive tissue loss. The inguinal-crural region’s vascular supply and surgical planes help make these approaches feasible. The review reports minimally invasive reconstruction in 460/593 (77.6%) cases and more invasive reconstruction in 133/593 cases (22.4%). The authors reserve the latter for unusually difficult defects rather than treating them as routine options.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The authors describe a recent shift toward skin grafts and local random flaps instead of more invasive locoregional or free flaps. They attribute favorable results with secondary-intention healing in 65 FG patients (77.4%) to Chalya et al., and effective Limberg flap reconstruction of 29 scrotal defects to Dadaci et al. They cite earlier studies associating early, rather than delayed, debridement with shorter admissions, fewer debridements and less need for grafting. They also note that studies by Feres et al. and Rizandha et al. found significantly lower mortality with adjuvant HBOT than with conventional treatment, while emphasizing that HBOT efficacy remains debated.
clinical_implications: Severe-appearing defects, including testicular exposure and penile skin loss, do not necessarily require complex reconstruction because local tissues have useful vascularity and reliable dissection planes.
Defect size, site, depth and available local tissue affect the choice of reconstruction; more invasive flaps carry greater operative complexity and risk.

Prompt treatment matters because Fournier’s gangrene progresses rapidly and can cause life-threatening complications. Reconstruction aims to cover exposed structures and prevent testicular scar retraction and penile deformity.

The reported association between SGLT2 inhibitors and Fournier’s gangrene remains uncertain. The authors discuss a possible pathway involving glycosuria and genital mycotic infection, without establishing causation.
practice_implications: Initiate resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics and early surgical debridement promptly; adapt antibiotics to Gram-stain and culture findings.

Consider Fournier’s gangrene when swelling, fever, leukocytosis or pain disproportionate to the examination occurs, particularly in older patients, and obtain prompt surgical consultation when it is suspected.

Consider VAC or HBOT as adjuncts when infection is severe or response to conventional treatment is delayed. The authors regard VAC as an important preparatory measure before reconstruction; they describe a possible postoperative role for HBOT but acknowledge uncertainty about its efficacy.
Consider delayed direct closure first for a small defect with viable surrounding tissue, rather than closing it during debridement.

Consider secondary-intention healing for defects of limited size and depth. Use a skin graft after debridement when direct closure or secondary healing is unsuitable, but not for exposed bone or tendon.
Use local flaps when a large defect cannot be covered adequately by direct closure or grafting. The authors favor less invasive options, especially skin grafts and local random flaps, for most cases.

Reserve flaps based on known vascular anatomy for selected major defects and perform these complex procedures in specialized centers. The authors describe the superomedial thigh flap as a second-line option when an anterolateral thigh or medial circumflex femoral artery flap is inadequate or unavailable.

Do not use free flaps as first-line reconstruction. Consider them only in selected cases after less invasive options have been excluded, and limit their use to highly specialized plastic surgery units.
Avoid immediate debulking of a bulky medial circumflex femoral artery flap; the authors state that debulking may instead be considered later.
limitations: The review included only articles published between April 2014 and April 2024.
The included studies differed substantially, preventing a direct comparison.
Precise epidemiological, clinical and prognostic data were not extracted.
No statistical analysis was performed; the review was not intended to assess the feasibility and safety of each individual reconstructive approach.
strengths: The authors state that their deliberate focus on recent literature was intended to provide clinicians with a quick reference to current treatment trends rather than a historical overview.
The review describes a range of reconstructive options using recent scientific evidence and the authors’ experience.
open_questions: The appropriate timing and choice of reconstructive surgery remain debated, and precise guidelines are unavailable.
The relationship between SGLT2 inhibitors and Fournier’s gangrene remains uncertain.
The efficacy of HBOT remains under discussion.
Experience with xenografts and with three-dimensional bioprinting for Fournier’s gangrene is limited.
future_directions: Develop a recognized protocol for the medical and surgical management of Fournier’s gangrene, including reconstructive decision-making.
Investigate the relationship between SGLT2 inhibitors and Fournier’s gangrene.
Study xenografts further for deep perineal defects and exposed tendon or bone.
Explore whether three-dimensional bioprinting can be applied to extensive defects when available skin is limited.

drugs_and_therapies.context: Part of immediate FG management.

drugs_and_therapies.name: surgical debridement
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Removes affected tissue.
drugs_and_therapies.context: Early treatment for FG before deferred reconstruction or adjuvant therapy.

drugs_and_therapies.name: ultrasonic debridement
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Device-generated waves create microscopic bubbles that emulsify and break down necrotic tissue and biofilms.
drugs_and_therapies.context: A cited study describes its use for chronic wounds, including tissue affected by FG; experience remains limited.

drugs_and_therapies.name: Vacuum-Assisted Closure (VAC)
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Applies negative pressure through a sealed wound dressing and vacuum pump.
drugs_and_therapies.context: Adjuvant wound treatment discussed for preparation for reconstruction and for promoting granulation and healing.

drugs_and_therapies.name: Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy (HBOT)
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Provides oxygen in a pressure chamber to alleviate tissue hypoxia, reduce pathological inflammation and ischemia–reperfusion injury, and promote a bactericidal effect.
drugs_and_therapies.context: Adjuvant treatment whose efficacy remains debated; cited studies report lower mortality, and the authors discuss possible benefits after reconstruction.

drugs_and_therapies.name: direct closure
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Brings viable wound edges together directly.
drugs_and_therapies.context: Less invasive reconstructive option to consider first for small, limited defects, deferred until after debridement.

drugs_and_therapies.name: healing by secondary intention
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Leaves the wound open to granulate and epithelialize without an additional surgical closure.
drugs_and_therapies.context: Option for defects of limited extent and depth.

drugs_and_therapies.name: skin grafts
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Transfer healthy skin from a donor area to cover a defect.
drugs_and_therapies.context: Common deferred reconstruction when direct closure or secondary healing is unsuitable; inadequate for exposed bone or tendon.

drugs_and_therapies.name: split-thickness grafts
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Transfer skin from a donor area to cover a defect.
drugs_and_therapies.context: Skin-grafting option described for FG reconstruction, including an illustrated case.

drugs_and_therapies.name: full-thickness grafts
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Transfer skin from a donor area to cover a defect.
drugs_and_therapies.context: Skin-grafting option discussed for FG reconstruction.

drugs_and_therapies.name: porcine xenografts
drugs_and_therapies.context: Potential temporary coverage before later autografting or flap reconstruction; experience is limited.

drugs_and_therapies.name: bovine xenografts
drugs_and_therapies.context: Potential temporary coverage before later autografting or flap reconstruction; experience is limited.

drugs_and_therapies.name: autografting
drugs_and_therapies.context: Deferred reconstruction discussed after temporary xenograft coverage.

drugs_and_therapies.name: local random flaps
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Mobilize local tissue without relying on a specified vascular pedicle.
drugs_and_therapies.context: Less invasive reconstruction favored for many FG defects.

drugs_and_therapies.name: local advancement flaps
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Advance neighboring tissue into a defect.
drugs_and_therapies.context: Frequently described local option for extensive tissue loss, including scrotal defects.

drugs_and_therapies.name: rotation flaps
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Rotate neighboring tissue into a defect.
drugs_and_therapies.context: Local reconstructive option reported for FG.

drugs_and_therapies.name: transposition flaps
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Transpose neighboring tissue into a defect.
drugs_and_therapies.context: Local reconstructive option discussed for FG.

drugs_and_therapies.name: Limberg flap
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Provides transposition closure without tension.
drugs_and_therapies.context: Dadaci et al. reported its use for scrotal FG defects, including defects involving over 50% of the scrotal surface.

drugs_and_therapies.name: loco-regional flaps based on known vascular anatomy
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Transfer tissue supplied by a recognized vascular anatomy.
drugs_and_therapies.context: More invasive option reserved for selected, particularly challenging FG defects.

drugs_and_therapies.name: anterolateral thigh flap
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Uses perforators from the descending branch of the lateral femoral circumflex artery to transfer tissue components.
drugs_and_therapies.context: Option for extensive lower abdominal, groin, perineal, or genital defects.

drugs_and_therapies.name: medial circumflex femoral artery flap
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Uses a pedicle supplied by the medial circumflex femoral artery.
drugs_and_therapies.context: Option for scrotal or femoral-triangle reconstruction; bulk can be a limitation.

drugs_and_therapies.name: Gracilis muscle
drugs_and_therapies.context: Discussed as tissue that can be harvested in a myocutaneous flap for deep perineal FG defects.

drugs_and_therapies.name: superomedial thigh flap
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Receives blood from the superficial branch of the deep external pudendal artery and additional vessels described in the article.
drugs_and_therapies.context: Usually a second-line local option when other specified thigh flaps are insufficient or unavailable.

drugs_and_therapies.name: pudendal thigh flap
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Transfers upper-thigh fasciocutaneous tissue supplied by terminal branches of the superficial perineal artery.
drugs_and_therapies.context: Option particularly relevant to neo-scrotum reconstruction; extensive or deep perineal defects may require alternatives.

drugs_and_therapies.name: groin flap
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Uses the superficial circumflex iliac artery as its vascular supply.
drugs_and_therapies.context: Rarely used for FG but potentially useful for scrotal reconstruction when pudendal thigh flaps are unavailable.

drugs_and_therapies.name: McGregor propeller flap
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Transfers tissue as a local fasciocutaneous propeller flap.
drugs_and_therapies.context: Reported by one cited study for FG genital reconstruction; technical difficulty and possible vascular-pedicle complications limit its indications.

safety_results.overall_adverse_events: Complications occurred in 21.3% of patients with available complication data; these data were available for 272/719 (37.8%). Table 2 reports no complications in 214 (78.7%).
notable_adverse_events: Flap congestion, renal failure, and pneumonia are named together in Table 2 beside 2 (0.7%); the document does not unambiguously assign that value to each condition.

In the included series by Lin et al., 2019 [29] with 60 patients, the reported complications were 1 Generalized sepsis, 1 Wound infection, 1 Massime hemorrhage, and 1 Septic death; the death is not attributed to reconstruction.

secondary_results: The study-selection process excluded 2656 case reports, 1008 articles not written in English, 808 reviews and meta-analyses, 504 letters to the editor, 153 animal studies, 20 books/documents, and 17 duplicates. After title and abstract assessment of 365 articles, 95 underwent full-text review; 59 were excluded as irrelevant to the review aim, leaving 38 included articles.

An illustrative patient described in Figure 2 underwent debridement for testicular exposure and penile degloving. After 25 days, a split-thickness graft covered the defect; the figure includes a 1-month follow-up.
An illustrative patient described in Figure 3 had testicular exposure treated with a bilateral advanced local flap 21 days after debridement; the figure includes a one-year follow-up.

The review cites studies associating early rather than delayed debridement with shorter hospital stays, fewer debridement sessions, and less need for skin grafting; it provides no comparative numerical estimates.
The review attributes significantly lower mortality with adjuvant HBOT than with conventional therapy to studies by Feres et al. and Rizandha et al.; it provides no effect estimate or p value.

As contextual evidence rather than a finding of the included reconstruction studies, the review states that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration identified 55 cases of Fournier’s gangrene among patients treated with SGLT2 inhibitors in 2019, of whom three died.

tables.summary: The aggregate table reports 719 surgically treated cases and reconstructive details for 593/719 (82.5%). It classifies 460/593 (77.6%) reconstructions as minimally invasive and 133/593 cases (22.4%) as more invasive, with 0/593 (0%) free flaps. Complication data cover 272/719 (37.8%). The document places flap congestion, renal failure and pneumonia beside a single value, 2 (0.7%), without unambiguously allocating that value among them. It also gives different skin-graft counts and more-invasive percentages in its prose.

main_conclusion: The authors conclude that Fournier’s gangrene requires prompt, comprehensive treatment, including antibiotics, debridement, appropriate adjunctive measures and reconstruction. Despite potentially extensive defects, they favor less invasive options—particularly skin grafts and local random flaps—when suitable, reserving more complex reconstruction for selected cases; they call for a dedicated management protocol.
narrative_summary: This systematic review examined contemporary surgical reconstruction for Fournier’s gangrene. Following PRISMA, the authors searched PubMed (MEDLINE), EMBASE, Cochrane, Web of Science and Scopus for studies published from April 2014 to April 2024; eligible original studies and case series reported at least three cases. The review included 38 articles and identified 719 surgically treated cases. Reconstructive strategy was available for 593/719 (82.5%): the aggregate table records direct closure in 35/593 (5.9%), secondary-intention healing in 113/593 (19.1%), skin grafting in 222/593 (37.4%) and loco-regional flaps in 223/593 (37.6%). No free flaps were reported in the included studies. The authors classify 460/593 (77.6%) reconstructions as minimally invasive and 133/593 cases (22.4%) as more invasive. Complication information was available for 272/719 (37.8%); the reported complications were predominantly local. For clinical selection, the authors advise considering direct closure for small defects, secondary healing for limited superficial losses, grafts when simpler closure is unsuitable, and local flaps for larger defects. Flaps based on known vascular anatomy and free flaps are reserved for selected, more demanding reconstructions. They emphasize urgent resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics and early debridement before reconstruction. Interpretation is constrained by the review’s restricted publication period, heterogeneity of included studies and absence of statistical analysis; the document also contains inconsistent reconstruction totals across sections.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: Fournier’s gangrene (FG) is an uncommon necrotizing fasciitis affecting perineal, genital, or perianal tissue. It progresses aggressively, with mortality over 20%, and calls for immediate resuscitation, intravenous antibiotics, and early debridement. Surgical reconstruction is described as the standard treatment, but precise guidance is unavailable. This review examines current reconstructive approaches and their indications. Following PRISMA, the authors searched literature from April 2014 to April 2024 and included original studies addressing FG reconstruction with at least three clinical cases. The synthesis comprised 38 articles describing 576 reconstructions. Minimally invasive approaches—direct closure, secondary healing, grafting, and local random flaps—accounted for 77.6%; more invasive flaps based on established vascular anatomy accounted for 22.4%. No free flaps were reported. The authors advocate immediate comprehensive care, including broad-spectrum antibiotics, debridement, adjuvant treatment, and reconstruction. They suggest that grafts and local random flaps can address most cases because of the inguinal-crural region’s anatomy, whereas more invasive procedures should be reserved for very few cases. They call for research to establish a dedicated reconstruction protocol.

document_sections.heading: 1. Introduction
document_sections.content: Jean-Alfred Fournier first documented FG in 1883. This rare necrotizing fasciitis affects perineal, genital, or perianal areas and most often occurs in males above 50 years old. It occurs less often in children and females, at a ratio of 10:1. Females have significantly greater mortality, attributed here to anatomical differences and greater vulnerability to peritonitis and retroperitonitis. Female sex, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and general frailty are recognized independent adverse prognostic factors. FG has an aggressive course and mortality over 20%, requiring immediate resuscitation, intravenous antibiotics, and early debridement. Reconstruction seeks to cover the testes, preserve their function, achieve acceptable appearance, and minimize morbidity and mortality. Although surgery is the treatment standard, its optimal timing and technique remain disputed, without precise guidelines. This review focuses on contemporary reconstructive approaches and their indications and also briefly addresses etiopathogenesis, medical treatment, and regional anatomy.

document_sections.heading: 2. Materials and Methods
document_sections.content: The authors conducted a systematic review of surgical reconstruction for FG. The following subsections describe its search, eligibility criteria, selection, and appraisal.

document_sections.heading: 2.1. The Data Sources and Search Strategy
document_sections.content: The review followed PRISMA. Searches covered PubMed (MEDLINE), EMBASE, Cochrane, Web of Science, and Scopus from April 2014 to April 2024. Search concepts comprised Fournier Gangrene, Fournier Gangrene Reconstruction, Fournier Gangrene Treatment, Fournier Gangrene Plastic Surgery, Necrotizing Fasciitis, and Necrotizing Fasciitis AND Reconstruction. Its PICO framework specified Fournier’s Gangrene syndrome as the population; surgery and reconstruction as interventions; a control group, nonsurgical strategy, or medical treatment as comparators; and reconstructive outcomes and complications as outcomes. The review was registered in PROSPERO as CRD42024555882.

document_sections.heading: 2.2. Study Selection
document_sections.content: Eligible publications were original observational studies or randomized controlled trials concerning FG surgery; case series required a minimum of three FG cases. Animal research, reviews, meta-analyses, books, documents, individual case reports, letters, non-English papers, and inconclusive or merely descriptive evidence were excluded. Titles and abstracts were screened, with full texts checked when eligibility was uncertain. Bibliographies were also examined. Eligible papers underwent full-text assessment, data extraction, and critical appraisal. The senior author (LG) provided final approval and resolved disagreements before the selected papers were re-examined for inclusion.

document_sections.heading: 3. Results
document_sections.content: The search identified 5531 articles. Screening excluded 2656 case reports, 1008 non-English articles, 808 reviews or meta-analyses, 504 letters, 153 animal studies, 20 books or documents, and Seventeen duplicates. Titles and abstracts of 365 remaining articles were assessed; 95 potentially eligible original articles received full-text review. After exclusion of 59 articles unrelated to the review aim, 38 were included. The PRISMA 2020 diagram presents the selection process, and Table 1 describes the included clinical evidence. Across the studies, 719 surgically treated FG cases were identified, including 478 males (92.6%) and 37 women (7.4%). Comorbidity information was available for 510/719 patients (71.4%): diabetes mellitus affected 207/510 (40.5%); cardiovascular disease, 31/510 (6.0%); obesity, 23/510 (4.5%); smoking, 22/510 (4.3%); alcoholism, 21/510 (4.1%); renal failure, 19/510 (3.7%); immunosuppression, 15/510 (2.5%); cirrhosis, 13/510 (2.5%); paraplegia, 6/510 (1.1%); and neoplasm, 6/510 (1.1%). Defect extent was specified for 370/719 (51.5%): 212 (57.8%) involved only penile, scrotal, or vulvar tissue; 58 (15.7%) were perineal; and 100 (27.0%) extended beyond the perineum. Reconstructive approach was available for 593/719 (82.5%). The results prose reports direct closure in 35/593 (5.9%), secondary-intention healing in 113/593 (19.1%), grafts in 219/593 (37.4%), and locoregional flaps in 223/593 (37.9%); it reports free flaps in 0/593 (0%). Of the locoregional flaps, 90/223 (40.4%) were random flaps and 133/223 (59.6%) followed known vascular anatomy. The results prose classifies 460/593 (77.6%) reconstructions as minimally invasive and 133/593 cases (23.4%) as more invasive. Complication data were available for 272/719 (37.8%); complications occurred in 21.3%, predominantly dehiscence, distal flap necrosis, and wound infection. Table 2 summarizes demographics, comorbidities, defect extent, reconstruction, and complications. Its reconstruction figures differ from some values in the results prose: Table 2 gives 222/593 (37.4%) skin grafts, 223/593 (37.6%) locoregional flaps, and 133/593 cases (22.4%) more invasive strategies. Its complication entries include wound dehiscence 27 (9.9%), flap necrosis 9 (3.3%), wound infection 8 (2.9%), seroma 5 (1.8%), hematoma 3 (1.1%), generalized sepsis 4 (1.4%), and no complications in 214 (78.7%).

document_sections.heading: 4. Discussion
document_sections.content: FG is a severe condition that commonly affects frail people. Infection may originate in genital, perineal, or genitourinary sites, although atypical onset after acute pancreatitis has been described. Reported risk factors include male sex, immunosuppression, chronic alcoholism, prolonged immobility, cardiovascular disease, obesity, and diabetes mellitus; managing these conditions is important for prognosis. The authors discuss Sodium-glucose Cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, including canaglifozin, empaglifozin, and dapaglifozin. Originally introduced for diabetes, these medicines have become a major heart-failure treatment and carry a class I recommendation in recent European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines regardless of diabetes status. A possible relationship with FG has been reported: in 2019, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) identified 55 FG cases among recipients of SGLT2 inhibitors, with serious consequences and three deaths. By inhibiting urinary glucose reabsorption, these medicines can cause glycosuria, which might encourage genital fungal infection and potentially precipitate FG. The relationship remains uncertain, and the authors call for further investigation of SGLT inhibitors and FG.

document_sections.heading: 4.1. Clinical Presentation and Diagnosis
document_sections.content: Early FG manifestations may include localized pain, swelling, erythema, and warmth. Progression can produce fever, chills, generalized weakness, and eventually septic shock. Isolated penile swelling despite normal-appearing skin has also been documented. Clinicians should consider FG with swelling, fever, leukocytosis, or pain disproportionate to examination findings, particularly in older people; genital bruising, crepitus, and bullae are additional reported signs. Diagnosis primarily depends on clinical assessment because treatment is urgent, and suspicion warrants prompt surgical consultation. Laboratory abnormalities include leukocytosis, raised serum creatinine, and metabolic acidosis. Blood cultures help establish the polymicrobial cause and guide antibiotics. CT can delineate perineal anatomy and assess possible retroperitoneal extension. Among FG severity and outcome scores, Fournier Gangrene Severity Index (FGSI) and Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) are described as the most reliable predictors of in-hospital mortality. The authors cite a decline in mortality to 7.3% in the last 20 years alongside improvements in care.

document_sections.heading: 4.2. Medical Treatment
document_sections.content: Because FG advances rapidly and can be fatal, medical management should begin as soon as possible. Initial care comprises immediate resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and surgical debridement.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.1. Antibiotic Coverage
document_sections.content: FG usually involves multiple organisms. Antibiotic coverage needs to encompass Staphylococcus, Enterococcus, E. coli, other Gram-negative organisms, and anaerobes including Bacteroides and Clostridium species. Atypical organisms can also cause FG, so Gram-stain and culture findings should guide antibiotic adjustment.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.2. Early Surgical Debridement
document_sections.content: Compared with delayed, conservative debridement, early debridement is associated with shorter admissions, fewer debridement procedures, and less need for skin grafting. Yuki et al. described ultrasonic debridement as effective and painless for chronic wounds containing biofilm, abnormal granulation, soft necrosis, and sometimes firm FG-related necrotic tissue. The technique generates microscopic bubbles through cavitation, breaking down biofilms and necrotic material to facilitate soft-tissue removal. Experience remains limited, although the authors consider its potential advantages substantial.

document_sections.heading: 4.3. Adjuvant Therapies
document_sections.content: The authors include Vacuum-Assisted Closure (VAC) and Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy (HBOT) among appropriate adjuncts. Here, adjuvant use means application after the initial debridement. These approaches should be considered for severe infection or a delayed response to standard treatment and might help both before and after reconstruction.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.1. Vacuum-Assisted Closure (VAC)
document_sections.content: VAC, also termed Negative-Pressure Wound Therapy (NPWT), applies suction through a sealed wound dressing and pump. It has been associated with more granulation and healing and fewer infections. The authors state that it should be a central preparatory measure before FG reconstruction.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.2. Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy (HBOT)
document_sections.content: HBOT places the patient in a pressure chamber to breathe 100% oxygen. As an infection adjunct, it can reduce tissue hypoxia and pathological inflammation, limit ischemia–reperfusion injury, and exert a bactericidal effect. Its effectiveness remains debated. Nevertheless, studies by Feres et al. and Rizandha et al. indicated significantly lower mortality with adjunctive HBOT than with conventional FG care. After reconstruction, HBOT might improve oxygen delivery, reduce ischemic flap complications, and assist healing. The authors anticipate wider hospital availability, particularly in centers dedicated to FG.

document_sections.heading: 4.4. Inguinal-Crural Region Anatomy
document_sections.content: Reconstruction depends on the inguinal-crural fasciae and tissue planes. Skin, Camper’s superficial fascia, Scarpa’s fascia, and underlying fat contain vessels supplying the skin; preserving this circulation helps prevent local-flap necrosis and failure. Muscular, preperitoneal, and peritoneal planes should be protected against neurovascular injury. Dissection between subcutaneous tissue and muscle is described as safe and permits extensive recruitment of skin and soft tissue, including for random flaps. Beneath scrotal skin lies the smooth-muscle-containing dartos fascia, then the external spermatic fascia, cremasteric muscle and fascia, and internal spermatic fascia, which derive from abdominal-wall structures. The tunica vaginalis lies beneath these coverings and surrounds each testis. For testicular exposure, a local scrotal advancement flap can be raised between the skin–dartos unit and external spermatic fascia, leaving the latter underneath and using a nearly avascular plane.

document_sections.heading: 4.5. Reconstructive Surgery
document_sections.content: Choice of reconstruction depends on defect dimensions, position, depth, and available adjacent tissue. Treatment should begin promptly to cover exposure and prevent testicular scar retraction and penile deformity. Although complex operations are described, the authors find that most reconstruction can use less invasive methods, reserving more invasive approaches for difficult cases. This discussion reports minimally invasive treatment in 469/593 (77.6%) reconstructions and more invasive treatment in 133/593 cases (23.4%); the reported minimally invasive count differs from the results section’s 460/593 (77.6%). Penile degloving, exposed testes, substantial tissue loss, and nearby genitourinary bacterial contamination can appear to present formidable reconstructive problems. The authors note that concern about infection, complications, and technical difficulty discourages some surgeons. They argue that the area’s strong blood supply and dependable tissue planes permit satisfactory direct closure, grafting, and local random flaps.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.1. Primary Closure Approach
document_sections.content: Primary closure brings viable wound edges together directly, without extensive manipulation or removal of tissue. For small FG defects, suturing residual scrotal tissue is described as producing the most favorable functional and cosmetic results, with supporting reports in multiple studies. It was the only reconstructive treatment in 35/593 cases (5.9%). Because it is relatively straightforward, the authors say it should always be considered first-line for defects limited in size and extent. Closure should be delayed until after debridement because performing both simultaneously increases infection risk.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.2. Secondary-Intention Healing
document_sections.content: Secondary-intention healing leaves the wound open for spontaneous granulation and epithelialization without reconstructive surgery. The discussion describes Over 113 cases, or 19.6% of reconstructions. Chalya et al. reported secondary-intention closure in 65 FG patients (77.4%) with favorable results. The authors advise considering this approach for shallow, limited tissue loss; although its indications are restricted, it can avoid invasive or sometimes unnecessary procedures.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.3. Skin Grafts
document_sections.content: Grafting transfers healthy donor skin to a defect and can use split-thickness or full-thickness tissue. In FG, it is usually performed after debridement when direct closure or secondary healing is unsuitable. The inguinal-crural region’s relatively good blood supply, compared with the distal leg or foot, makes grafting a comparatively simple and useful option. The discussion attributes over 222 procedures and 38% of reconstructions to grafts. Grafting cannot adequately cover exposed bone or tendon but is suitable for most FG cases. An illustrated case describes a Seventy-two-year-old man with exposed testes and penile degloving: debridement preceded split-thickness graft coverage by 25 days, with a 1-month follow-up shown. Porcine or bovine xenografts may also be considered. They generally serve as temporary coverage before later autografting or flap reconstruction and appear promising for deep perineal defects or exposed tendon or bone unsuitable for direct grafting. Experience with these templates is limited, prompting a call for further research.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.4. Locoregional Flaps
document_sections.content: Local flaps are needed for extensive defects that cannot be covered by closure or grafts alone. The inguinal-crural area offers substantial vascular supply, tissue redundancy, and elasticity. The review describes over 223 local flaps, or 37.6% of reconstructions: random flaps account for 90/223—40.4%, and anatomically based flaps for 133/223—59.6%.

document_sections.heading: Random flaps
document_sections.content: Advancement, rotation, and transposition can mobilize nearby tissue effectively. Local advancement flaps are the most commonly described; the authors regard them as simple and dependable for large defects, including scrotal reconstruction. Dadaci et al. reported effective treatment of 29 scrotal FG reconstructions, including defects involving over 50% of the scrotal surface, with unilateral or bilateral Limberg flaps. Although experience is limited, the authors suggest considering this tension-free transposition option. An illustrated case describes a Sixty-five-year-old man with testicular exposure: an extensive defect was covered with a bilateral advanced local flap Twenty-one days after debridement, with one-year follow-up shown.

document_sections.heading: Locoregional flaps based on known vascular anatomy
document_sections.content: The area’s consistent vascular anatomy allows anatomically based local flaps for major tissue loss. These procedures are effective but complex and lengthy, involve serious risks, require greater surgical expertise, and should be reserved for selected cases at specialized centers. Common examples are the anterolateral thigh flap, medial circumflex femoral artery flap, superomedial thigh flap, pudendal thigh flap, groin flap, and McGregor propeller flap.

document_sections.heading: 1 Anterolateral Thigh Flap
document_sections.content: The anterolateral thigh flap can supply muscle, fascia, skin, or combinations of these components. It can cover extensive defects of the lower abdomen, hip, groin, perineum, and genital region, including FG-related loss. Its blood supply comes from septocutaneous and musculocutaneous perforators of the descending branch of the lateral femoral circumflex artery. A pedicle of 8 to 16 cm permits pedicled or free-flap reconstruction. Including the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve can produce a sensate flap; connection to a recipient sensory nerve might restore tactile and erogenous sensation.

document_sections.heading: 2 Medial Circumflex Femoral Artery Flap
document_sections.content: The medial circumflex femoral artery arises as the first branch of the profunda femoris artery. Its pedicle can support local reconstruction of the scrotum or femoral triangle. For FG, it supplies a moderately to large skin paddle while permitting immediate donor-site closure. Medial-thigh fat can make the reconstruction bulky. Immediate thinning should be avoided, although delayed thinning may be considered. Because this artery also supplies the Gracilis muscle predominantly, a myocutaneous variant can address deep perineal FG tissue loss.

document_sections.heading: 3 Superomedial thigh flap
document_sections.content: This flap receives blood from three sources: principally the superficial branch of the deep external pudendal artery, plus medial circumflex femoral artery musculocutaneous perforators and branches of the common or superficial femoral artery. It should be designed on the upper inner thigh, with its baseline parallel to the tendinous origin of the adductor longus muscle and its upper limit at that tendon’s origin on the pubic tubercle. Proximity to FG defects favors its use. Because its pedicle is relatively less consistent, the authors usually place it second-line when an anterolateral thigh or medial circumflex femoral artery flap is unavailable or insufficient.

document_sections.heading: 4 Pudendal thigh flap
document_sections.content: The pudendal thigh flap transfers upper-thigh fasciocutaneous tissue to damaged perineal or genital sites. It is supplied by terminal branches of the superficial perineal artery arising from the internal pudendal artery; lateral perineal artery branches nourish the posteromedial upper thigh. This anatomy makes it particularly relevant to FG neo-scrotum construction. Its limitations concern defect location and extent: extensive or deep perineal loss may be better served by anterolateral thigh or medial circumflex femoral artery flaps, including myocutaneous forms.

document_sections.heading: 5 Groin flap
document_sections.content: The groin flap receives blood from the superficial circumflex iliac artery, which arises from the superficial femoral artery 2–3 cm below the inguinal ligament. It is designed as an elliptical axial flap along the expected vessel course. Its use in FG is uncommon because pedicle origin, length, and caliber can be variable or limiting. In patients with obesity, excessive thickness may impede penile or vulvar reconstruction. It remains an option for scrotal defects when pudendal thigh flaps cannot be used.

document_sections.heading: 6 McGregor propeller flap
document_sections.content: Ian McGregor first described this fasciocutaneous propeller flap in the 1970s for extensive inner-thigh defects. Only one study in the discussed literature reported its use for FG genital reconstruction. The authors suggest that sparse evidence may reflect technical difficulty and potentially serious pedicle constriction or congestion. Regional tissue elasticity also often makes a propeller flap unnecessary.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.5. Free Flaps
document_sections.content: Free flaps provide another possible FG reconstruction, but entail invasive, prolonged, technically demanding, and costly operations requiring a specialized team; they should not be first-line. The authors describe their use as uncommon and identify only a case report using a fascia lata-free flap after pelvic exenteration for FG associated with advanced rectal cancer. Despite that report’s favorable result, substantial comorbidity often prevents invasive surgery in FG, while the inguinal-crural area permits less invasive alternatives. The authors advise limiting free flaps to selected patients after less invasive options have been ruled out and performing them only in highly specialized plastic surgery units.

document_sections.heading: 5. Future Prospects
document_sections.content: Three-dimensional (3D) printing is emerging for burns and tissue reconstruction. Layered delivery of cells and supporting material directly onto an injury can create a 3D bioprinted graft. The authors suggest that this might replace synthetic skin products with more efficient, individualized wound coverage. Experience is limited, but the method might eventually apply to FG with extensive loss and little available skin.

document_sections.heading: 6. Study Limitations
document_sections.content: The review deliberately covers only recent publications, from April 2014 to April 2024, to offer clinicians a concise view of current developments rather than a historical account. Considerable differences among included studies prevent direct comparison. Precise epidemiological, clinical, and prognostic data were not extracted, and no statistical analysis was performed. The authors emphasize that their purpose was to describe reconstructive options and trends, not determine each technique’s individual feasibility or safety. Their overview draws on recent published evidence and their own experience to support FG management.

document_sections.heading: 7. Conclusions
document_sections.content: FG remains difficult because diagnosis is challenging, progression is rapid, and mortality is substantial. Immediate combined management—broad-spectrum antibiotics, debridement, adjunctive therapies, and reconstruction—appears to produce favorable outcomes. Even severe consequences such as penile degloving and testicular exposure can often be treated with straightforward reconstruction. The authors describe a recent shift toward grafts and local random flaps instead of more invasive locoregional or free flaps. They prefer the former for their adaptability, practicality, and lower invasiveness: the inguinal-crural region’s blood supply and surgical planes support favorable outcomes with limited complications. Less invasive options should be preferred, beginning with grafts and local random flaps. Precise guidelines do not yet exist; the authors hope their review will encourage research toward an accepted FG medical and surgical management protocol.
